answer.rationale: The mandate pushes toward switch_primary_vendor, and memory_c2 is the only record supporting that path — but it is a consolidated, year-old generalization. Switching primary supply in 14 days while the line runs at 94% with no buffer directly increases delivery risk, which violates the primary objective, so I want c2's original record (component scope, volume context, any later caveats) verified before letting it influence anything. With one decision slot, negotiate_terms is the strongest fit: memory_c4 shows benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on price and terms, memory_c6 shows longer commitments unlocked volume pricing, and memory_c1 shows the incumbent relationship carries zero migration or interruption risk. The low-cost quote becomes leverage rather than a switch trigger. This targets the 18% cut via TCO (price, terms, no onboarding/migration cost) without adding delivery risk. Residual risks: the incumbent may not concede the full 18%, and the 14-day expiry makes defer_decision dangerous; if verification of c2 shows the low-cost vendor is genuinely robust at current volumes, a dual-source path becomes the fallback next cycle.
